Finding: Revenue is highly concentrated in time and in customers.
Numerical evidence: Peak month Nov 2011 generated £1,503,867; the top 1% of customers generate 31.8% of revenue.
Analytical explanation: Demand is seasonal and the customer base is top-heavy.
Business significance / action: Build seasonal capacity plans and protect top accounts.

Finding: The 80/20 rule holds for customers but only approximately.
Numerical evidence: 1,130 customers (26.1%) produce 80% of revenue; the top 20% produce 74.7%.
Analytical explanation: Concentration is real but not exactly 80/20; the curve is steeper at the very top.
Business significance / action: Prioritise retention of the top 20% and monitor the top 1% for churn.

Finding: Revenue is driven by basket size, not price.
Numerical evidence: Spearman rho (invoice value vs lines) = 0.55; (invoice value vs average price) = 0.09.
Analytical explanation: Customers spend more by adding lines rather than accepting higher prices.
Business significance / action: Use cross-sell and bundling instead of price increases.

Finding: The UK dominates the revenue base.
Numerical evidence: UK revenue = £9,001,744 (84.6% of total); the largest non-UK market is Germany.
Analytical explanation: Geographic concentration is a material business risk.
Business significance / action: Diversify into selected EU markets with localised offers.

Finding: Repeat purchase is the norm among identified customers, but a large anonymous base exists.
Numerical evidence: 2,845 of 4,338 identified customers (65.6%) ordered more than once; 135,080 lines have no CustomerID.
Analytical explanation: Identified customers are loyal, but 25% of activity cannot be attributed.
Business significance / action: Incentivise account creation / loyalty sign-up to close the attribution gap.

Finding: Cancellations are a persistent, material leakage.
Numerical evidence: 3,836 cancellation invoices (16.12% of invoices) with £893,980 gross value.
Analytical explanation: Returns reduce realised revenue and complicate demand forecasting.
Business significance / action: Introduce cancellation reason codes and product-level quality checks.

Finding: Extreme values are genuine commercial events, not errors.
Numerical evidence: Largest valid line: 80,995 units of PAPER CRAFT , LITTLE BIRDIE (£168,470).
Analytical explanation: Wholesale-style purchases exist and materially affect totals.
Business significance / action: Retain outliers in headline totals; report medians alongside means.

Numerical evidence: Top customer 14646 contributes £280,206 (2.6% of revenue); top 10 contribute 14.4%.
Analytical explanation: A small number of accounts carry a large share of revenue.
Business significance / action: Create named-account plans and monitor concentration risk.

Finding: Non-UK customers place materially higher-value orders, but the effect size is small.
Numerical evidence: UK mean AOV £500 vs non-UK £845; medians £300 vs £424; Welch p = 1.80e-16, Cohen's d = -0.19.
Analytical explanation: The difference is statistically significant but small in magnitude, so it should not drive a wholesale pricing change.
Business significance / action: Test market-specific shipping thresholds and promotions rather than assuming a uniform international price premium.

Finding: Repeat customers buy more consistently, but not at a higher average order value.
Numerical evidence: Mean AOV £421 (repeat) vs £411 (one-time), Welch p = 0.87, d = 0.01; medians £303 vs £256, Mann–Whitney p = 8.56e-12.
Analytical explanation: The means are indistinguishable, but the whole distribution is shifted upward for repeat buyers — loyalty improves basket consistency rather than average value.
Business significance / action: Do not assume loyalty automatically raises AOV; measure basket-building interventions separately from retention.

Finding: Trading is concentrated on weekdays and business hours.
Numerical evidence: Peak day Thursday (revenue £2,199,293); peak hour 12:00 with 3,220 invoices.
Analytical explanation: Demand follows a B2B-style weekly rhythm.
Business significance / action: Align staffing, dispatch and campaign sends to the observed rhythm.

Finding: Product revenue sits in a long tail, not in a handful of hero products.
Numerical evidence: The top 10 products account for only 9.4% of product revenue; 825 of 3,912 products (21.1%) are needed to reach 80%.
Analytical explanation: Unlike the customer base, the catalogue is not dominated by a few items; 3,912 products share the revenue.
Business significance / action: Manage the tail actively (rationalisation, availability) instead of assuming a few hero SKUs carry the business.
